(a) 'A staged proposal takes no effect as a declaration' follows by instantiating AXM-commit-is-approval, but 'take effect' is defined nowhere. DEF-proof-state treats a staged lemma or branch exactly like a declared one, so it can be proven and cited. The only effect the premises reserve to declarations is grounding: a root must be a declared axiom or definition. If the clause is meant to also cover something else, such as a staged branch supporting a decision, that needs its own premise. (b) DEF-proof-state says the state is computed from 'place in the premise graph and the trials alone', yet its proven condition also uses a declared minimum and a declared consensus. This clause does not break, because the subject is explicitly excluded, but the 'alone' is looser than it reads. (c) 'Keeps its proof state' holds only when the loss of the subject is the sole change. A commit that removes the subject and also restates a premise will move the state, through the restatement.

reasoning: Built scenarios that satisfy every premise and tried to break each clause. Acyclicity: (a) a node that cites itself; (b) two declared nodes that cite each other; (c) one id declared at head and also staged in the ledger with different citations, to try to get an edge into a node admitted earlier. None of these gives a cycle. Under DEF-premise-graph an edge is added only when a node is admitted, and it comes only from premises already in the graph. So every edge runs from an earlier-admitted node to a later one, and an admission order is a topological order. In (a) and (b) no node is ever admitted. In (c) the id is admitted once and its edges still point forward. LMA-kernel-enforces-acyclicity states the same result for every build. Never proven: (d) a branch citing a lemma that cites nothing. That lemma is a root and not a declared axiom or definition, so DEF-proof-state blocks the proof. (e) a branch citing nothing. DEF-proof-state requires at least one cited premise. (f) a branch whose only root is an axiom staged in the ledger and not declared. DEF-proof-state requires the root to be a DECLARED axiom or definition. (g) a branch whose ancestry passes through a cycle or a missing premise. It is never admitted, so under DEF-proof-state it has no proof state and is never proven. (h) an infinite descending citation chain, where every ancestor has premises and so there are no roots at all. That would satisfy the root clause vacuously. It cannot happen: admission is sequential and each premise is admitted before its dependent, so a chain N0 <- N1 <- N2 ... would need admission times that decrease forever, and they cannot. Every backward path therefore ends at a node that cites none. Each attack fails.

Clause 1: DEF-premise-graph itself defines the premise graph as the graph the kernel builds on every read and gives the build procedure, so this clause restates a declared definition. Clause 2 is LMA-kernel-enforces-acyclicity applied to every read. It also follows directly from DEF-premise-graph's admission rule, since edges go only from earlier to later admissions. Premise-to-dependent edges are directed, so the 'strictly directed and acyclic' of AXM-acyclicity is met. Clause 3: I read 'ancestry' as the set of nodes a node depends on under DEF-premise-graph. This is the only graph notion the premises supply, and the derivation rule uses the two terms interchangeably. Its 'ends' are the dependencies that cite nothing. There are two cases. If the node is not admitted, DEF-proof-state gives it no proof state and it is never proven. If it is admitted, some root is not a declared axiom or definition, or the node cites nothing. Either way it fails a conjunct of DEF-proof-state. The clause holds under both readings of 'does not end in': 'some root is not an axiom/definition' and 'no root is'. 'Ungrounded' only labels the case that AXM-axiomatic-grounding forbids. No outcome depends on it. The claim asserts one direction only and does not claim that grounded nodes are proven. I found no unstated assumption.

NOT(claim) needs one of three things: (i) the kernel builds the graph other than as DEF-premise-graph defines; (ii) some build contains a cycle; (iii) some lemma or branch whose ancestry has a root that is not a declared axiom or definition is proven. (i) contradicts the declared definition. (ii) contradicts LMA-kernel-enforces-acyclicity and the admission-order argument. (iii) contradicts DEF-proof-state, whose 'exactly when' makes every such root disqualifying. No disjunct can be derived from the cited premises, so they decide the claim.

Split the claim into three clauses and tried to break each while keeping every cited premise true. (1) Never edited or removed: DEF-ledger says trials are entries in the append-only ledger, and append-only means existing entries are neither changed nor deleted. The scenario 'an amendment rewrites the trial' fails because an amendment is its own appended entry. (2) Only-when clause: I looked for a change C where a trial is current before C and not current after it, yet no amendment is appended and nothing in {T} ∪ anc_before(T) ∪ anc_after(T) is restated or removed. DEF-current-trial has three conjuncts, and I tried to flip each. (a) Validity: by that definition it is the trial's own validity after amendments appended to it, and the trial cannot be edited, so it changes only when an amendment is appended. (b) Membership in the graph: DEF-premise-graph's build always ends with the same set, namely the nodes whose citation chains are well-founded (induction on rank). So if T and every ancestor keep their citations and stay declared or staged, T stays in the graph. Leaving the graph needs a removal, a dangling citation or a cycle, and each of those needs a restatement or removal inside {T} ∪ anc_before. (c) Fingerprints: the ancestor set is fixed by the citations of T and its ancestors. So a changed ancestor set or a changed fingerprint means some node in {T} ∪ anc_before ∪ anc_after changed its statement or citations, which DEF-restatement calls restating. The fingerprint is injective on (statement, citations), so an accidental match cannot hide a change. Declaring a new node N: if T cited N, directly or through an ancestor, then T was not in the graph before, so its trial was not current. So a declaration cannot end currentness. Declaring an id that was already staged is a restatement. A change that restates several nodes at once still includes a qualifying node, because the argument above uses the definitions directly and does not compose single-node lemma steps. Weakest attack: a node moves in one change from declared-only to staged-only with a new statement. If 'stays declared or staged' is read as '(stays declared) or (stays staged)', the node is neither restated nor removed, yet its fingerprint changes. This fails on the natural reading. DEF-restatement pairs 'restated' (stays in the declared-or-staged set) with its complement 'removed' (in neither), so the move counts as a restatement. (3) If a scenario meets DEF-counterexample against the present premises, every premise holds in it and the claim fails. So those premises do not entail the claim. I found no premise-satisfying scenario that refutes any clause.

Each clause follows from cited premises without code knowledge. Clause 1 follows from DEF-ledger's 'append-only'. Clause 2 follows from DEF-current-trial, whose three conjuncts depend only on (i) validity after appended amendments, (ii) membership in the graph and (iii) fingerprints of T and its ancestors. DEF-premise-graph makes membership and ancestry functions of the declared and staged nodes' citations alone. DEF-restatement names every change of statement or citations of a present node, and every disappearance. LMA-blast-radius-propagation's third clause agrees for single-node changes, but it is not needed: the direct argument also covers changes to several nodes at once. The step that most needs checking is 'validity changes only by an appended amendment'. It rests on reading 'its validity, after any amendments appended to it' as the trial's own validity, fixed because the trial is immutable, then modified only by amendments. That is the plain reading of the definition, not an outside assumption. If the author wants no room for doubt, DEF-current-trial could say outright that nothing other than an appended amendment changes a trial's validity. Clause 3 is the semantic definition of non-entailment applied to DEF-counterexample: all premises are satisfied and the claim fails. I found no step that needs an uncited premise.

I tried to derive the negation of each clause from the same premises. NOT(1), 'some recorded trial is edited or removed', contradicts DEF-ledger's append-only ledger. NOT(2) needs a trial to stop being current with no appended amendment and no restatement or removal of T or its before/after ancestors. The counterexample trial shows that none of DEF-current-trial's conjuncts can flip that way under DEF-premise-graph and DEF-restatement. The only reading that yields NOT(2) is the split parse '(stays declared) or (stays staged)' of DEF-restatement, and that parse leaves some node moves outside both 'restated' and 'removed', which the definition's pairing of the two terms rules out. NOT(3) would need a scenario that satisfies all premises and falsifies the claim, yet the premises still entail the claim, which is impossible under any sound notion of 'follows'. The premises decide the claim.

counterexample: Missing definition: the posterior over a contract slice is conditioned on that slice's belief-eligible trials alone. No trial outside the slice may enter it, whether pooled directly or through a prior fitted to other slices. This is the posterior counterpart of what DEF-contract-slice already states for sufficiency ('counted over that slice's trials alone').
reasoning: Clauses 1-3 held up. Clause 1 is AXM-no-belief-write-path restated. A counterexample to it would have to change a slice posterior with something that is not belief-eligible, such as a human statement, which breaks that axiom. Clause 2 is LMA-asserted-is-inert applied to slice posteriors, since AXM-no-belief-write-path identifies a measured belief with the posterior over a slice. Clause 3: I tried a contract-level verdict that is sufficient over the pooled trials while each slice is below its sufficiency. That verdict is on a different claim, so it does not contradict 'a slice issues no verdict'. Under DEF-contract-slice a slice is its own claim with sufficiency counted over its own trials, and AXM-sparse-data-no-verdict then blocks the slice's verdict. Clause 4 does not hold. Contract C declares compatibility key {firmware}. Slice S1 (firmware=A) has 3 belief-eligible trials, all passed. Slice S2 (firmware=B) has 50 belief-eligible trials, 10 passed. The measured belief for S1 is the posterior over S1's pass rate, but it is conditioned on S1 and S2 together: fully pooled as Beta(1+13, 1+40), or partially pooled through a prior fitted to S2. Every cited premise holds. S1 and S2 are separate slices under DEF-contract-slice, and S1's sufficiency is still counted over its 3 trials alone. S1's posterior changes only through belief-eligible trials, because DEF-contract-slice treats eligibility as a property of a trial on the contract, not of a slice. No asserted record is involved. Yet trials that differ on firmware are pooled into one measured belief. I do not record this as a falsification, because it depends on reading 'the posterior over a contract slice' as 'a posterior ABOUT the slice' and not 'a posterior conditioned ONLY ON the slice's trials'. The cited premises never define that phrase. A second, narrower wording issue: the claim says 'a declared compatibility key' without saying which contract declares it. Read broadly, it fails when two trials on C2 differ on a key that only C1 declares. The derivation rule narrows it to the contract's own key, and I judged it under that reading.

counterexample: Unstated premise: a slice's posterior is conditioned on that slice's own belief-eligible trials alone, with no evidence from any other slice, directly or through the prior.
reasoning: Clauses 1-3 follow with no extra assumption: 1 from AXM-no-belief-write-path, 2 from LMA-asserted-is-inert, 3 from DEF-contract-slice together with AXM-sparse-data-no-verdict. Clause 4 does not follow. The derivation rule argues that trials differing on a compatibility key fall in different slices (true by DEF-contract-slice), that a measured belief is the posterior over one slice (AXM-no-belief-write-path), and 'so they are never pooled'. That last step silently assumes a posterior over one slice draws only on that slice's trials. DEF-contract-slice limits a slice's MEMBERSHIP and its SUFFICIENCY COUNT to its own trials. It says nothing about what evidence the slice's posterior is conditioned on. AXM-no-belief-write-path only requires that evidence to be belief-eligible, and trials from a sibling slice are belief-eligible. So pooling or partial pooling across slices is consistent with every cited premise.

NOT(claim) would need a derivation of one of four things: a slice posterior moving through non-eligible evidence, an asserted record moving a belief, a verdict below sufficiency, or pooling across compatibility-key values. The first three contradict AXM-no-belief-write-path, LMA-asserted-is-inert and AXM-sparse-data-no-verdict with DEF-contract-slice. The fourth cannot be derived either. The premises allow pooling but do not require it: in a model where each slice's posterior is conditioned only on its own trials, every premise holds and so does the claim. Clause 4 is undecided, not refuted. That shortfall is recorded once, as the entailment gap; no premise supports the negation.

Tried one concrete scenario per clause. (1) Posterior moved by something other than evidence: an asserted record, or a new trial that is not belief-eligible, is attached to slice S and S's posterior shifts. LMA-asserted-is-inert and AXM-no-belief-write-path both rule this out, since the slice posterior is the measured belief the axiom names. A variant where the contract's declared prior is edited and S's posterior shifts with no new evidence either breaks the axiom ('changes only through belief-eligible evidence') or, if prior edits are not counted as changes of belief, leaves the claim's wording just as intact as the axiom's. The clause adds nothing beyond the axiom, so any scenario that violates the clause also violates a premise. (2) Sparse slice with a verdict: contract C has slice A with 100 trials and slice B with 3, the threshold is 30, and B issues a verdict because C's pooled count is 103. DEF-contract-slice counts sufficiency over B's trials alone (3 < 30), B is a claim of its own, and AXM-sparse-data-no-verdict then forbids the verdict. A contract-level verdict would not be one that B issues, so it does not violate the clause. (3) Pooling across the compatibility key: trials t1 (key k=x) and t2 (k=y) enter one posterior. Three routes tried. (a) One slice holding both: impossible, since a slice requires the same value on every key. (b) Slice A's posterior uses a prior fitted from slice B's trials (empirical-Bayes leakage): DEF-contract-slice says nothing from another slice enters it. (c) A contract-wide pooled figure passed off as a measured belief: AXM-no-belief-write-path identifies a measured belief with the posterior over a contract slice, and a union of two slices is not a contract slice. Edge cases also checked: an empty compatibility key (trials cannot differ on it, so the clause holds vacuously); a trial with no value for a key (it is in no shared slice with a trial that has one, so it is not pooled); overlapping condition buckets (every slice still has uniform key values). None of these satisfies every premise while breaking the claim.

Clause 1: the slice posterior is a measured belief because AXM-no-belief-write-path equates the two. Given that, 'only through belief-eligible evidence' comes directly from the axiom and 'never through an asserted record' comes directly from LMA-asserted-is-inert. The term 'belief-eligible' is used exactly as the axiom uses it and never unpacked, so DEF-belief-eligible does not need to be cited. Clause 2: DEF-contract-slice makes each slice a claim of its own, with its verdict on that slice and its sufficiency counted over its own trials. AXM-sparse-data-no-verdict, applied to that claim, gives no verdict below the declared sufficiency. If no sufficiency is declared, the clause holds vacuously. Clause 3: DEF-contract-slice says trials that differ on any key of the compatibility key are in different slices. AXM-no-belief-write-path says a measured belief is the posterior over a contract slice, and DEF-contract-slice says that posterior uses only its own slice's trials and the declared prior, with nothing from another slice. So no measured belief pools such trials. The only assumption I could find is reading the axiom's dash-apposition ('A measured belief -- the posterior over a contract slice --') as an identification rather than an example. That is its plain grammatical reading, and the derivation rule relies on it explicitly, so I do not count it as a hidden premise. No clause needs knowledge of the implementation.

NOT(claim) would need one of three things: a slice posterior that moves through non-eligible or asserted input, a below-sufficiency slice that issues a verdict, or trials differing on the compatibility key pooled into one measured belief. Each is contradicted directly by a cited premise (the axiom plus LMA-asserted-is-inert; DEF-contract-slice plus AXM-sparse-data-no-verdict; DEF-contract-slice plus AXM-no-belief-write-path). So the negation could only be derived if the premises were inconsistent. I looked for an inconsistency. The candidate is DEF-contract-slice (the posterior depends on the declared prior) against AXM-no-belief-write-path (the belief changes only through evidence, and a human's statement carries zero weight). These conflict only if a declared prior can change, or if a declaration counts as a 'statement by a human', and no cited premise asserts either. AXM-sparse-data-no-verdict's allowance for a labelled estimate is not a verdict, so it does not conflict with clause 2. The premises do not derive the negation.

Attack: a reporting component that saves its report (a file with a hash) and records it in the ledger as an imported trial, citing the monitor as its source, against a contract a declared test can measure. Every premise holds: DEF-belief-eligible admits any imported record that has a source, an artifact and a hash, and nothing in it excludes a report. The posterior for that contract slice would move, and the node the trial is recorded on would have its proof state recomputed. I did not record this as falsified because the claim fails only if 'reporting' includes writing a ledger record. The act of reporting alone, a read over the ledger and declarations that produces output, writes no record. Under that reading AXM-no-belief-write-path and DEF-proof-state leave belief and proof state unchanged. So the attack exposes a term the claim never defines rather than a clean refutation. That problem belongs to the entailment trial.

counterexample: Missing premise: a report (the reporting component) only reads the ledger and the declarations and appends no record of any provenance to the ledger, in particular no trial on any node and no measured or imported record, and it changes no declaration. As a declared axiom or definition, this would let the 'neither belief-eligible nor a trial' clauses follow. As written, the claim leans on CTR-monitor-read-only, which is implementation fidelity and not a premise.
reasoning: The derivation says 'a report is neither [measured nor imported]' and 'a report is not a trial recorded on any node' without deriving either. No cited premise constrains what a reporting component writes. DEF-ledger lists what the ledger holds; it does not say a report adds nothing to it. DEF-belief-eligible does not rule out an imported record whose artifact is a report. DEF-proof-state makes proof state depend on the trials recorded on a node, so a component that records a trial changes it. The only support offered is 'evidence: CTR-monitor-read-only', which is a component-belief contract about the implementation, not a declared premise. The claim therefore rests on an uncited fact about the component: that it appends nothing to the ledger, in particular no trial record of any provenance, and changes no declaration.

Tried to derive NOT(claim), that some report changes a belief or a proof state. No cited premise says a report writes a trial or an imported or measured record. The premises also directly give that any finding written as a statement is asserted (DEF-belief-eligible) and carries zero weight (AXM-no-belief-write-path). So the negation is not derivable. The premises cannot derive the claim's positive clauses either, but that is the entailment gap recorded above. It does not make NOT(claim) derivable.

Attacks tried, all with every premise held. (1) A report that alters or deletes an existing artifact so a hash no longer matches: DEF-report only forbids appending, but DEF-ledger makes the ledger, artifacts included, append-only, so the alteration is excluded by a cited premise. (2) A report that writes a record kind DEF-ledger does not list, such as a staged proposal or a withdrawal: DEF-report forbids appending 'no record', and the list after it is illustrative, not exhaustive, so this is excluded. (3) A report that moves git HEAD or edits the working tree: moving HEAD changes which declarations load, and DEF-report's 'changes no declaration' covers that; a working-tree write is not a declaration. (4) An existing imported record becoming or ceasing to be belief-eligible because its contract changed: that needs a declaration change, which is excluded. (5) A report's finding being counted as weight: AXM gives zero weight to statements by agents and humans, and a reader is neither, but the axiom's first clause (belief moves only through belief-eligible evidence, meaning trial records) already covers it, because a report is not a record. (6) A report changing the premise graph through repository state other than the declarations: this is the strongest attack, but no cited premise says what the graph is built from, so I cannot show that this scenario satisfies the premises. The hole belongs under entailment, and it is not a realizable falsification. No scenario survived.

counterexample: Missing premise: that the premise graph and the builds that admit its nodes are determined only by the declarations (at git HEAD) and the staged proposals recorded in the ledger. This could be DEF-premise-graph, cited with that content. The claim also needs that a node's current trials are determined only by the ledger and the declared statements.
reasoning: The belief half follows: AXM-no-belief-write-path plus DEF-belief-eligible (evidence is a trial record) plus DEF-ledger plus DEF-report (no record appended, and the ledger is append-only) give 'no measured belief moves'. The proof-state half does not follow. DEF-proof-state says a proof state is computed from the node's place in the premise graph and its trials, and that a node no build admits has none. It never says what the premise graph is built from or what a build admits. The step 'the premise graph is built from the declarations and the staged proposals' appears in no cited premise, and DEF-premise-graph is not cited. So the premises leave open that a report changes the graph or its admission through repository state that DEF-report does not forbid it to write (it forbids only ledger appends and declaration changes). A smaller point: 'current trials' in DEF-proof-state is not defined by any cited premise, so the claim that a report cannot change which trials are current also rests on an unstated premise.

NOT(claim) requires deriving that some report does change a belief or a proof state. For belief this is contradicted outright: DEF-report plus AXM-no-belief-write-path forbid it. For proof state the premises are silent on how the graph is built, so they derive neither the claim nor its negation. Nothing cited asserts that a report affects the graph or the trials. The undecided part is already reported as the entailment gap, and NOT(claim) is not positively derivable.

Attacks tried, each with every premise held. (1) A report that deletes or overwrites a captured artifact, so a measured record points at a missing artifact. This fails in two ways. DEF-ledger makes artifacts part of an append-only ledger, so the scenario breaks a premise. And even if the premises allowed it, DEF-belief-eligible's 'captured its artifact with the artifact's hash' describes how the record was made, not whether the artifact exists now, so the record stays eligible and AXM-no-belief-write-path allows no other route. (2) A report that moves the repository head to a revision with a different consistency.yaml. Under DEF-report that counts as changing a declaration, so the output is not a report. (3) A belief that drifts with time or with priors while a report runs. AXM-no-belief-write-path allows change only through belief-eligible evidence, and a report changes no declaration anyway. (4) A premise graph that depends on the order nodes are admitted, so rebuilding it could give a different graph even with unchanged inputs. Under DEF-premise-graph the admitted set is the unique least fixpoint: a node whose premises are all admissible must be admitted before the build can end, and no node is admitted before its premises. Edges come only from citations, so equal inputs give an equal graph. (5) A node's declared minimum or consensus changing. Both are declarations or staged-ledger content, and a report changes neither. No scenario survived.

I checked each step against the exact wording. The rationale's paraphrase of DEF-report is faithful. So is its paraphrase of DEF-proof-state ('its place in the premise graph and the trials recorded on it alone'). For DEF-premise-graph it quotes the graph's inputs verbatim, and it correctly concludes that the graph is unchanged when the declarations and staged proposals are unchanged, which holds because the build is deterministic. For DEF-current-trial it lists all three conditions, and adds that the fingerprints are fixed by statements and cited premises, which the report leaves unchanged. Two links are implicit but derivable, not gaps. (a) The step that makes a belief-eligible trial record a ledger record: DEF-ledger lists trials among the records the servers keep, and DEF-belief-eligible's provenance population includes notes, which are ledger records. (b) The rationale leaves out the declared minimum and consensus from DEF-proof-state's proven condition. Both are declarations, or ledger content for a staged node, so no report changes them. DEF-proof-state's claim to be computed 'from nothing else' sits uneasily with its own use of declared thresholds, but that tension is inside the premise and does not affect this claim.

To derive NOT(claim), a report would have to move a belief or a proof state. A belief moves only through belief-eligible evidence, which is an appended trial record (AXM-no-belief-write-path, DEF-belief-eligible, DEF-ledger). Every input to a proof state is either a declaration or a ledger append: the graph, the trials, their amendments, fingerprints and thresholds. DEF-report forbids a report from changing either one. None of the premises gives a way for output returned to a caller to become an input to either computation, so the negation cannot be derived.

Attack 1 (the restatement): does losing the subject change the input DEF-proof-state now names, the node's own declaration? No. DEF-proof-state lists what that declaration contributes (statement, cited premises, declared sufficiency) and then excludes 'nothing else belief.yaml or the ledger says about it, its subject included'. The subject is not in that list, and belief.yaml losing a component does not edit the branch's own declaration. Attack 2: can the branch fall out of the graph? DEF-premise-graph admits a node once every premise it cites is in the graph, and a build ends only when every node left out cites a missing premise. A subject is not a citation, so the branch must still be admitted. AXM-no-silent-failure's wording 'not dropped in silence' might allow a reported drop, but DEF-premise-graph's end condition rules it out. Attack 3: can its trials stop being current? DEF-current-trial's fingerprint is statement plus cited premises, neither of which changes, the target stays in the graph and validity is untouched. Attack 4: a single commit that deletes the subject and also restates an upstream premise leaves the branch STALE. That change comes from the premise, not from losing the subject, and the claim, read with its derivation rule ('losing it changes neither...'), is about the subject's removal alone. None of these attacks satisfies every premise and breaks the claim.

Each clause traces to a cited premise. Graph admission: DEF-premise-graph (from head declarations and staged proposals only, no other step adds a node). A staged proposal is not a declaration: AXM-commit-is-approval. Reporting of unadmitted nodes and of branches whose subject is gone: AXM-no-silent-failure. 'Cannot take its place' matches 'no build admits'. Proof state kept: the DEF-proof-state inputs (graph place, own declaration's statement, premises and sufficiency, trials) with the subject explicitly excluded, together with DEF-current-trial's subject-free fingerprint and DEF-premise-graph's citation-only edges. The rationale's paraphrase of the restated DEF-proof-state is faithful. It lists the same three inputs and the same declaration components and keeps the subject exclusion. It drops only the wider 'nothing else belief.yaml or the ledger says' clause, which this step does not need. Sufficiency is sourced from the node's own declaration, not from the subject, so no unstated premise is required.

Deriving NOT(the branch keeps its proof state) would need losing the subject to change the branch's graph place, one of its own declaration's three components, or which of its trials are current. The subject is excluded by name from the proof-state inputs, is not an edge, and is not part of any fingerprint, so none of these can be derived. The negations of the other clauses (an unadmitted node dropped silently, a staged proposal acting as a declaration, a node entering from elsewhere) contradict AXM-no-silent-failure, AXM-commit-is-approval and DEF-premise-graph directly.

subject: BRN-consistency-declarations-gate
text: Wording, not a verdict: the claim says 'that branch keeps its proof state' without the qualifier its derivation rule carries ('losing it changes neither...'). One commit that both deletes the subject and restates an upstream premise leaves the branch STALE, which the literal claim does not allow. If the author wants the claim to be exact, it could read 'losing its subject does not change that branch's proof state'. A second, smaller point: AXM-no-silent-failure says 'not dropped in silence', which on its own would allow a drop that is reported. Only DEF-premise-graph's end condition rules that drop out.

reasoning: Attacks tried, each keeping every premise true. (1) The new input, the node's own declaration or staged proposal: a report restating or withdrawing a staged proposal. By DEF-premise-graph a staged proposal lives in the ledger, and by DEF-ledger the ledger is append-only records, so staging, restating or withdrawing one means appending a record. DEF-report forbids appending any record, of any provenance, so this fails. Editing a declared node's statement, cited premises or declared sufficiency is a declaration change, which DEF-report also forbids. (2) Moving HEAD to another revision, e.g. a checkout or reset, without editing a file, so the declarations at the head revision differ. Under the only reading on which the kernel's input differs, this changes a node's declaration as the graph sees it, so DEF-report excludes it. If the declarations are identical, the graph is identical. (3) Writing an artifact into the ledger. DEF-ledger lists artifacts apart from records, so DEF-report's 'no record' might not cover them. But no premise makes a proof state, a trial's currency or a belief depend on an artifact on its own: belief moves only through a trial record (AXM plus DEF-belief-eligible), and proof state is closed under DEF-proof-state's 'from nothing else'. So this fails too. (4) The report's finding is later imported as evidence with the report as artifact. That import is a separate act that appends a record. It is not producing the report, and the claim is about producing it. (5) Changing which trials are current through a new amendment or fingerprint drift. Amendments are records, and fingerprints depend on statements and citations, which are declarations or proposals. Both are excluded. No scenario survives.

The rationale's paraphrase of DEF-proof-state ('its place in the premise graph, its own declaration or staged proposal, and the trials recorded on it') matches the restated wording. It omits the parenthetical (statement, cited premises, declared sufficiency) and the 'from nothing else' closure. The argument still goes through, because it covers each of the three inputs, and the closure it needs is in the premise as cited. Each input is fixed by a cited premise: the graph by DEF-premise-graph plus DEF-report (no declaration change, no record appended, so no proposal staged); the own declaration or proposal by DEF-report plus DEF-ledger/DEF-premise-graph (proposals are ledger records, and the ledger is append-only); trials and their currency by DEF-current-trial (validity after amendments, graph membership and fingerprints are all unchanged). For beliefs, AXM-no-belief-write-path plus DEF-belief-eligible (only trial records count) plus DEF-report (appends none) settle it. One soft spot is that 'staging a proposal is appending a ledger record' is inferred from DEF-premise-graph's 'proposals staged in the ledger' together with DEF-ledger's 'records'; no premise states it. I judge it entailed, not assumed.

Deriving NOT(claim) would need some input to a proof state or a belief that a report can change. DEF-proof-state closes the input set ('from nothing else'), and AXM closes the belief write path. DEF-report fixes every member of both sets: records, declarations, proposals, and through them the graph and trial currency. DEF-report's last clause ('Output that does either is not a report') also makes any change-producing output fall outside the claim's subject by definition. No premise supplies a channel from which the negation follows.

Tried every way a lemma or branch could reach a proof state without grounding in axioms or definitions. (a) It cites nothing: DEF-proof-state requires at least one cited premise, so it is not proven. (b) It cites a premise that is missing, withdrawn or never staged: DEF-premise-graph never admits it, and DEF-proof-state says a node with no build has no proof state and is never proven. (c) A citation cycle, including a node citing itself: no member of the cycle ever has all its premises present, so none is admitted. (d) An ancestor that is a lemma or branch citing nothing: it is a node the claimant depends on that cites none and is not an axiom or definition, so the claimant is not proven. (e) Roots that are partly axioms and partly not: the 'every' clause fails. (f) The restated inputs (statement, cited premises, declared sufficiency, trials): enough passing trials cannot make up for the grounding conjunct, because 'proven exactly when' is a conjunction and grounding is one of its terms. Acyclicity: LMA-kernel-enforces-acyclicity gives it, and DEF-premise-graph also forces it on its own, since every edge runs from an earlier-admitted node to a later one. The strongest attack is a node that exists as both a HEAD declaration and a staged proposal with different citation lists. The graph admits one version and the cites-at-least-one check reads the other. For example, the admitted version is a root lemma citing nothing, so it has no dependencies and the 'every dependency' clause holds vacuously, while the declaration cites an axiom. That would make an ungrounded node proven. The premises do not rule this reading out, but they do not force it either, so it is recorded as the entailment gap and not as a counterexample that satisfies every premise.

counterexample: Missing premise: a node has exactly one citation list per build. Either a declaration and a staged proposal with the same id are one node whose admitted version is the one DEF-proof-state reads, or the premises fix a precedence between them. Without this, a node can be admitted as a root lemma citing nothing and still pass the 'cites at least one premise' check through its other version.
reasoning: Acyclicity follows from LMA-kernel-enforces-acyclicity (and from DEF-premise-graph alone). 'Ungrounded implies never proven' follows from the grounding conjunct of DEF-proof-state together with its no-build clause. But the restated DEF-proof-state reads the cited premises from 'its own declaration or staged proposal'. DEF-premise-graph builds edges from what the admitted node cites, and admits declarations and staged proposals each 'at most once' without saying whether a declared id and a staged proposal with the same id are one node, or which version wins. The claim's step 'cites a premise and every dependency that cites none is an axiom or definition, therefore its ancestry ends in axioms or definitions' holds only if the citation list the proof state reads is the same one the graph admitted. A secondary point, not scored: the opening clause 'the proof kernel builds the premise graph as DEF-premise-graph defines' holds only by stipulation, because the definition names the kernel's build. Whether the kernel actually conforms is component-belief's question.

Tried to derive NOT(claim): either a build that contains a cycle, or a proven lemma or branch whose ancestry ends outside axioms and definitions. A cycle contradicts LMA-kernel-enforces-acyclicity and the admission order in DEF-premise-graph. A proven ungrounded node is only permitted, never forced, under the version-ambiguity reading above. Under the natural reading of one node with one citation list, it contradicts DEF-proof-state. The premises therefore do not derive the negation. The weakness is underdetermination, which is already recorded as the entailment gap, not a derivable contrary.

Attack (two-version, reshaped): lemma L is declared at head citing X, where X is in neither the head nor the ledger, and L is also staged as a proposal that cites nothing. Read literally, DEF-premise-graph builds from the declared nodes AND the staged proposals, and a build cannot end while a left-out node cites only premises already in the graph. So the staged L, which cites nothing, is admitted, the declared L can never be admitted, and 'each at most once' then keeps it out for good. L then has no in-edges. If DEF-proof-state read the declaration, L would 'cite at least one premise' (X), the depends-on check would pass vacuously, and an L with no grounded ancestry would read as proven. The attack does not hold up as a counterexample, though. DEF-proof-state says outright that the version the build admitted is the declaration for a declared id, and in this scenario the build admitted the staged version, so the scenario breaks a cited premise. Other attacks, all blocked: a self-citing node is never admitted because its premise is never in the graph first. A staged 'axiom' that cites nothing is not a declared axiom, so it grounds nothing. A definition that cites an ungrounded root U fails because U is a lemma that cites none. Cycles are ruled out by LMA-kernel-enforces-acyclicity and by the rule that a node is admitted only after its premises. No scenario that satisfies every premise breaks the claim.

counterexample: Missing premise (DEF-premise-graph): a node is identified by its id. For an id declared at head, the build considers only the declaration as a candidate, and a staged proposal with that id is neither a candidate nor admitted. A staged proposal is a candidate only for an id not declared at head. With this, the edges and the cited-premise list read by DEF-proof-state always come from the same version.
reasoning: The new wording removes the ambiguity inside DEF-proof-state: for an id declared at head, the declaration is read. It does not close the two-version attack across the two definitions. DEF-proof-state asserts which version the build admitted, but DEF-premise-graph, which defines the build, never says it. That definition takes both declarations and staged proposals as input, admits each 'node' at most once, and never says whether a node is an id or a version, or that a declaration shadows a staged proposal with the same id. Its termination rule can even force the staged version in when the declaration cites a missing premise. DEF-proof-state takes 'cites at least one premise' from the version it names, while the depends-on check uses the graph's edges, which come from whichever version was actually admitted. The step that no ungrounded lemma or branch reads as proven therefore holds only if the premise below holds.

Attempted: derive a cycle or a proven ungrounded lemma/branch. A cycle contradicts LMA-kernel-enforces-acyclicity. For a declaration-only or proposal-only id, the edges and the citations come from the one version, so the root check in DEF-proof-state forbids the ungrounded case. The only route to NOT(claim) is the both-versions case, and that needs the build to admit the staged version of a declared id. The premises neither force this (DEF-proof-state says the declaration is the admitted version) nor forbid it outright. NOT(claim) is therefore not derivable either. The weakness is underdetermination, already recorded as the entailment gap, not a proof of the negation.

subject: BRN-dag-integrity
text: Two-version attack after the DEF-proof-state restatement: the ambiguity has moved, not closed. DEF-proof-state now names the declaration as 'the version the build admitted', but DEF-premise-graph (which defines the build) admits from declarations and staged proposals, counts 'each node at most once' without saying whether a node is an id or a version, and never says a declaration shadows a staged proposal with the same id. Its termination rule ('ends only when every node left out cites a premise not in it') can force the staged version in when the declaration cites a missing premise. Suggested fix for the author: state the shadowing in DEF-premise-graph, not only in DEF-proof-state.

reasoning: Attack: id X is declared at head as a lemma citing P, where P is not in the graph, so the declaration can never be admitted. A staged proposal with the same id X cites only axioms. DEF-premise-graph builds from declarations AND staged proposals, and a build ends only when every node left out cites a missing premise. If staged X counts as a candidate node, the build has to admit it. Then declared nodes citing X get admitted on the staged statement, so the staged proposal would act as the declaration. Also, the id X is in the graph, so the stuck declaration might never be reported. The attack fails as a counterexample because it breaks a premise. DEF-proof-state's appositive fixes the version the build admitted: for an id declared at head that version is its declaration, and a staged proposal is the version only for an id not declared there. A build that admits staged X for a declared X therefore violates DEF-proof-state, so the scenario does not satisfy every premise. I also tried a branch whose subject was dropped from belief.yaml. A subject is not a citation (DEF-premise-graph) and is not part of the fingerprint (DEF-current-trial), and DEF-proof-state reads nothing else about the node, subject included. Its place in the graph and its current trials are unchanged, so it keeps its proof state. No scenario satisfying every premise breaks the claim.

counterexample: Unstated premise: DEF-premise-graph must say that a staged proposal whose id is declared at the head revision is not a candidate for admission (the declaration shadows it whether or not the declaration itself is admissible), and that nodes are identified by id. Otherwise a stuck declaration can be masked by an admissible staged proposal with the same id: the declaration goes unreported and the proposal stands in its place.
reasoning: The claim 'a staged proposal takes no effect as a declaration' and the reporting clause both depend on the build never admitting a staged proposal whose id is declared at head. That rule appears only as an appositive in DEF-proof-state (which version a proof state reads). It is not a rule of the build: DEF-premise-graph builds from head declarations and staged proposals without excluding a shadowed proposal, and 'each at most once' does not say whether a node is identified by id or by version. As premises are worded, DEF-premise-graph's termination condition (every node left out cites a missing premise) can require admitting a staged X whose declared X is stuck, while DEF-proof-state requires the admitted version of X to be the declaration. The claim holds only through the precedence stated in DEF-proof-state, and nothing makes the build follow it. The paraphrase in the derivation rule matches DEF-proof-state's new wording, except that it drops 'and from nothing else belief.yaml or the ledger says about it'. The rule's step about keeping the proof state needs that dropped clause, although it is in the premise.

NOT(claim) would need one of these to be derivable: (a) something other than head declarations or staged proposals enters the graph, which DEF-premise-graph excludes; (b) a staged proposal takes effect as a declaration, which AXM-commit-is-approval excludes, and DEF-proof-state's precedence keeps a declared id reading its declaration; (c) an unadmitted node or a subjectless branch is silently dropped, which AXM-no-silent-failure excludes; (d) a subjectless branch loses its proof state, which DEF-proof-state rules out because it reads nothing about the subject. The shadowing ambiguity found in the entailment trial produces a conflict between premises, not a derivation of the negation, so the premises do not also entail NOT(claim).

Attacks tried. (1) Change which version the build admits: under DEF-proof-state that is the declaration at the head revision, or a staged proposal for an id not declared there. A report changes no declaration (DEF-report). Staging, restating or withdrawing a proposal puts content into the ledger, and DEF-ledger makes the ledger append-only records, so each of those is an appended record, which DEF-report forbids. (2) Move the head revision, e.g. a reader that checks out another commit: if that commit's declarations differ, the node's declaration at the head revision has changed, which is a changed declaration in the sense DEF-premise-graph and DEF-proof-state use, so that output is not a report. If they do not differ, no input changes. (3) Change the trials on a node, or which of them are current: that needs an appended trial or amendment, or a changed fingerprint, which needs a changed statement or citation. All are excluded. Rewriting a record in place, or damaging an artifact, contradicts DEF-ledger's append-only. (4) Move belief by a finding such as 'evidence stale': the finding is output, not a record, so it has no provenance. Existing records keep their eligibility, because DEF-belief-eligible fixes eligibility at recording, and the contract/test declarations are unchanged. (5) The report's other writes, which the rule concedes ('whatever else it reads or writes'): DEF-proof-state lists its inputs, and none of them is anything a report may write. No scenario satisfies every premise and falsifies the claim.

Beliefs: AXM-no-belief-write-path plus DEF-belief-eligible (a trial record) plus DEF-report (no record of any provenance) gives no new eligible evidence, so no belief moves. Proof states: every input DEF-proof-state names (place in the graph; the admitted version with its statement, cited premises and declared sufficiency; the trials recorded on it) is fixed. The graph is fixed by DEF-premise-graph because declarations and staged proposals are unchanged. Currency is fixed by DEF-current-trial because there are no new trials or amendments, the graph is the same, and the fingerprints are the same. The rule's paraphrase of DEF-proof-state is faithful to the new wording on the admitted version (head declaration, else staged proposal) but drops two clauses: 'with that version's statement, cited premises and declared sufficiency', and the exclusivity clause 'and from nothing else belief.yaml or the ledger says about it'. Without exclusivity, 'so no proof state changes' does not follow from the rule's own text. It does follow from the cited premise itself, so this is a flaw in the prose, not a missing premise. One reading was weighed and rejected: the exclusivity is scoped to belief.yaml and the ledger, but the positive list of inputs already fixes what the state is computed from.

To derive NOT(claim) one needs a report that alters some input of a belief or a proof state. DEF-report forbids appending any record and changing any declaration. DEF-ledger (append-only) forbids in-place rewrites. DEF-proof-state and AXM-no-belief-write-path name no input a report can otherwise touch. No derivation of the negation exists from these premises.

subject: BRN-monitor-moves-nothing
text: The derivation rule paraphrases DEF-proof-state without its exclusivity clause ('and from nothing else belief.yaml or the ledger says about it') and without 'with that version's statement, cited premises and declared sufficiency'. The step 'so no proof state changes' leans on exclusivity, so the rule should state it. Two smaller points. (a) That clause limits its exclusion to belief.yaml and the ledger, so exhaustiveness rests on reading the positive input list as the complete list. (b) 'Changes no declaration' in DEF-report is taken to cover moving HEAD to a commit with different declarations; nothing defines 'declaration' so as to say that explicitly.

reasoning: Attacks tried. (1) Self-citation: node X cites X. X is admitted only once every premise it cites is already in the graph, and X is not there before its own admission. Nodes are identified by id and admitted at most once, so X is never admitted and adds no edge X->X. (2) Two versions of one id citing each other: a declared X that cannot be admitted, plus a staged X' that cites X. A staged proposal is not a candidate for an id declared at head, so X' is never a candidate. If X is not declared and two staged proposals share id X, the node is the id, and it is admitted at most once. A second version citing the first needs X already in the graph, and then X cannot be admitted again. So at most one version is present and no edge links two versions. (3) A declared id that can never be admitted stays out of the graph, and so does everything citing it. Being out adds nothing, since only admission adds edges. (4) An edge added later that leaves an earlier node: every edge added with m ends at m, and every premise of m was admitted before m. So every edge runs from an earlier admission to a later one. Admission order is a topological order and no cycle can form. No scenario that keeps every premise produces a cycle.

The claim follows from four clauses of DEF-premise-graph. The build starts empty and admits one node at a time. Nodes are identified by id, each admitted at most once and never removed. Admission requires every cited premise to be present already. Only admission adds a node or an edge, and the edges it adds run from the premises to the new node. Together these give an invariant: every edge points from an earlier admission to a later one, so the graph is acyclic at every step, whether the build is finished or not. The candidate-selection and termination clauses are not needed, so no unstated assumption about which version is chosen or whether the build ends is carried in. Uncited assumptions are excluded from edges by definition, and the claim is scoped to edges.

Deriving 'some build contains a cycle' would need an edge from a node to one admitted before it, or a node admitted twice. The premises rule out both: a cited premise must be present before admission, admission is at most once per id, and only admission adds edges. The premises decide the claim affirmatively, so NOT(claim) cannot be derived.

Replayed the previous attack: lemma L is declared at head citing X, where X exists nowhere, and L is also staged citing nothing. Under the new DEF-premise-graph, L's head declaration is its only candidate 'whether or not it can be admitted', so the staged version is not a candidate. X is never in the graph, so L is never admitted, and by DEF-proof-state L has no proof state and is never proven. The attack fails. Other attacks tried: (a) a staged lemma S with an undeclared id that cites nothing, and a branch B that cites S. Both are admitted, but S cites none and is not a declared axiom or definition, so B is not proven; S itself cites no premise, so it is not proven either. (b) A staged 'definition' with an undeclared id used as a root. DEF-premise-graph consistently contrasts 'declared at the head revision' with 'staged in the ledger', so a staged node is not 'declared' and cannot serve as a grounding root. (c) Self-citation and mutual citation. Admission needs every cited premise to be in the graph already, and each node is admitted at most once, so neither can be admitted. (d) Admission-order dependence. Each id now has exactly one candidate and admission is monotone, so the admitted set is the unique least fixpoint whatever the order. I found no scenario in which every premise holds and the claim fails.

The step 'no cycle, as AXM-acyclicity requires' is exactly LMA-kernel-enforces-acyclicity. For groundedness: a node outside the graph is never proven (DEF-proof-state). Inside the graph, the graph is finite and acyclic, and a node's only incoming edges come from its citations, so every ancestry ends at an admitted node that cites none. Proof requires each such node to be a declared axiom or definition, so an ancestry that ends anywhere else is never proven. DEF-premise-graph and DEF-proof-state now agree on the version read: the head declaration for a declared id, and the staged proposal only for an id not declared at head. This closes the earlier gap. Residual wording note, not a gap: DEF-proof-state's 'declared axiom or definition' relies on DEF-premise-graph's usage of 'declared' to mean declared at the head revision, which is the only reading the premises support.

NOT(claim) would need either a build containing a cycle, which contradicts LMA-kernel-enforces-acyclicity, or a proven lemma or branch with a root that is not a declared axiom or definition, which contradicts the 'exactly when' condition of DEF-proof-state. With one candidate per id, the premises no longer leave room for a second admitted version that could make the negation derivable.

Attack 1 (declaration appears): id X has only a staged proposal P, admitted. A declaration D of X is committed and P stays staged. Under DEF-premise-graph the node is its id X, and D is now its only candidate, so the node X has been restated from P's content to D's. That is the lemma's own subject, so the case is covered, not missed. If D differs, fp(X) changes, and every trial that recorded fp(P) for X is not current (DEF-current-trial requires the recorded set to equal the current one). If D cannot be admitted, X leaves the graph. X is then not 'removed' in the lemma's sense (it is still declared), but clause 1 still holds: X's own trials fail the target-in-graph condition, and dependents lose X from their current dependency set. Clause 1 says nothing about trials that recorded fp(D), so it is not contradicted. Attack 2 (declaration disappears, P still staged): P becomes the candidate. This is the same analysis, and it is a no-op when P and D have identical statement and citations. Attack 3 (restate a staged P that a declaration shadows): P is not a candidate for X, so node X's admitted version and fingerprint do not change. Reading this as 'r restated' would make clause 1 false, because trials recording fp(D) would stay current while differing from fp(P'). But DEF-premise-graph makes the node its id with the declaration as its only candidate, so a shadowed proposal is not a version of r, and the scenario does not restate r. Attack 4, on clause 3: can a candidate switch for X change the admission of some e that depends on X in neither build? It cannot. Citations are by id, other ids' candidates are unchanged, and the least-fixpoint build admits e together with its ancestor set (none of which is X) identically, with the same fingerprints. No scenario satisfying all premises breaks the claim.

Clause 1 follows from DEF-current-trial. The recorded fingerprints must be exactly the current ones, and a recorded fp(r) that differs from r's current fingerprint makes the sets unequal, whether r is still a dependency or has dropped out. Clause 2 follows from DEF-premise-graph. With neither a declaration nor a staged proposal, r has no candidate, so r is never admitted. Induction along a citation path from r shows no dependent is admitted either, because every other id keeps the same candidate and the same citations. A trial whose target is not in the graph is not current. Clause 3 also follows. The build's result is fixed by the admission and end conditions. An e with no path from r has an ancestor set that excludes r, and that set is admitted identically in both builds, so e's membership, dependencies and fingerprints are unchanged, and so is the currency of each of its trials. Pre-fingerprint trials depend only on validity and graph membership, and both are unchanged. The new precedence rule adds no unstated assumption, because it only fixes which version the single id r has. The step reads 'restated' as a change to the version that is r's candidate, and DEF-premise-graph's 'a node is identified by its id' supplies that reading.

NOT(claim) would need one of three things: a trial that recorded a stale fp(r) and is still current, which contradicts DEF-current-trial's exact-match condition; a removed r, or one of its dependents, being admitted, which contradicts the rule that a node with no candidate cannot be admitted and the rule that a node is admitted only after its cited premises; or a node that is independent of r in both builds whose currency flips, which contradicts the unchanged candidates and citations of every id other than r. None of these can be derived from the premises.

subject: LMA-blast-radius-propagation
text: The lemma never defines 'restated'. The step holds only if 'r is restated' means that the version which is r's candidate changes in content, which includes a declaration of r appearing or disappearing while a staged proposal for r exists. If restating a staged proposal that a declaration shadows counted as restating r, clause 1 would fail: trials that recorded the declaration's fingerprint would stay current while differing from the proposal's new fingerprint. DEF-premise-graph's 'a node is identified by its id; the declaration is its only candidate' excludes that reading, so I recorded no gap. The author may want the claim to say 'r's candidate is restated or changes' to make this explicit.

reasoning: Attacks tried. (1) Beliefs: can a report make existing evidence stop being belief-eligible? Eligibility depends on provenance (fixed per record), on the artifact and its hash, and on a declared test being able to measure the contract. A report appends no record and changes no declaration, and the ledger holding the artifacts is append-only by DEF-ledger. So the set of belief-eligible evidence is unchanged, and by AXM-no-belief-write-path no belief moves. A finding in a report is output, not a record, so it carries no weight. (2) Proof states: can a report change which candidate the build admits for an id? Declared ids have exactly one candidate, their declaration, and a report changes none. Undeclared ids take candidates from the staged proposals, and a report stages none. Fingerprints depend on statements and citations, and currency depends on amendments and graph membership; none of these changes. (3) Strongest attack: stage two proposals for one undeclared id X, P1 and P2. The premises allow this: DEF-premise-graph says a staged proposal is a candidate for an undeclared id and does not say there is only one. Because 'each at most once' is counted per id, a build admits only one of them, and which one depends on order. The report's own read then builds afresh and could admit P2 where an earlier read admitted P1, giving X a different proof state. I did not record this as falsified. The difference comes from any fresh read, not from producing a report, and the report changed no input. So no scenario found in which the report causes the change; the order-dependence is recorded under entailment.

counterexample: Missing premise: for an id not declared at the head revision, at most one staged proposal is a candidate (for example, restating a proposal supersedes the earlier one, or the latest one staged is the only candidate). Equivalently: the premise graph is determined by the declarations at head and the staged proposals, whatever order the build admits them in. DEF-premise-graph would need to state this for 'the graph is unchanged' to follow from 'the report changes no input'.
reasoning: The belief half follows from DEF-report, DEF-belief-eligible, DEF-ledger and AXM-no-belief-write-path. The paraphrases in the rule match the current wording: DEF-premise-graph's inputs, and DEF-proof-state's admitted version and its 'nothing else' clause, which the rule quotes minus 'its subject included'. That omission does not affect the argument. The gap is the step 'the graph is unchanged' and 'neither which version a build admits nor that version changes'. That step needs the build's result to be a function of its inputs. DEF-premise-graph gives this only when each id has at most one candidate. For declared ids it does: the declaration is the only candidate. For an id not declared at head, it allows any staged proposal as a candidate and does not rule out several; the rule itself speaks of proposals being 'restated'. With two admissible candidates for one id, 'admits each at most once' makes the admitted version depend on build order. Then two builds from identical inputs, including the one the report's own read performs, can differ. DEF-proof-state's singular 'its staged proposal' hints at uniqueness but does not state it.

Tried to derive that producing a report changes a belief or a proof state. Nothing in the premises gives a report any path to either. By DEF-report it appends no record of any provenance and changes no declaration. AXM-no-belief-write-path closes every non-evidence route to belief. DEF-proof-state excludes everything belief.yaml or the ledger says beyond the admitted version and its trials. The order-dependence found under entailment lets a rebuild differ, but it does not make that difference an effect of producing a report. So NOT(claim) is not derivable, only left open by that one gap.

Replayed the previous attack. Declared X cites P, which can never be admitted; a staged proposal also named X cites only axioms. Under the new DEF-premise-graph the declaration is X's only candidate because X is declared at head. The staged X is not a candidate, so X is left out. The build still ends, since the one left-out candidate cites P, which is not in the graph. AXM-no-silent-failure then requires X (the declared node that cannot take its place) to be reported, and the staged X is reported by the same axiom as a staged node that cannot take its place. The stuck declaration can no longer be hidden. Second attack: two staged proposals B1 and B2 share an undeclared id B, both can be admitted, and they have different statements and trials. Successive builds may admit different versions, so B's proof state can change between reads. That change is caused by version selection, not by the subject being lost, so the claim that losing the subject does not alter the proof state survives. It is recorded as a gap under entailment. Third attack: a branch whose belief.yaml subject is removed. Admission depends only on cited premises, and fingerprints depend only on statement and premises. DEF-proof-state excludes the subject, so neither the branch's place in the graph nor its current trials change. No scenario satisfying every premise made the claim fail.

counterexample: Missing premise: for each id not declared at the head revision, the ledger stages at most one live proposal (or the definition names which one is the candidate). Without it, two staged proposals Y1 (citing a premise that is never admitted) and Y2 (citing only axioms) with the same id Y let Y2 be admitted while Y1 is never reported. Y1 is not reported because the node Y, identified by its id, took its place.
reasoning: The replayed gap is closed: one candidate per declared id makes a stuck declaration unhidable, and the added 'from nothing else ... its subject included' clause carries the proof-state-stands step. The remaining unstated assumption is for undeclared ids. DEF-premise-graph says 'a staged proposal is a candidate', and DEF-proof-state says 'its staged proposal' (singular), but no cited premise says the ledger holds at most one staged proposal per id, or which one is admitted if there are several. With two staged proposals for the same undeclared id, the build admits whichever becomes admissible first. A stuck version can then be shadowed by an admitted one of the same id (the old hiding pattern, moved to the ledger), and the version that 'the build admitted' is not fixed from one read to the next. The claim's reporting clause and its proof-state clause both rely on that version being unique.

NOT(claim) would need one of four things: a node entering the graph from outside head declarations or staged proposals (DEF-premise-graph forbids any other step that adds a node), a staged proposal taking effect as a declaration (AXM-commit-is-approval forbids it), a stuck declared or staged node, or a subject-less branch, going unreported (AXM-no-silent-failure forbids it), or the subject entering the proof state (DEF-proof-state excludes it). None of these follows from the premises, so the negation cannot be derived.

Attack: id X is staged with statement B, admitted, and is the target (or an upstream premise) of trial T. (a) A declaration of X with statement A, or citing a premise not in the graph, is committed. By DEF-premise-graph the declaration becomes X's only candidate, so X's fingerprint changes or X leaves the graph, and T stops being current. (b) The reverse case: X is declared with A and a staged B also exists, then the declaration is deleted, so B becomes the candidate. In both cases X is never removed in DEF-restatement's sense, because it stays declared or staged throughout. It is 'restated' only if a node's statement is that of its current candidate. Since DEF-premise-graph now makes the id the node, that is the natural reading, and under it both cases are restatements of X, which the claim lists. A declaration with the same text as the staged proposal changes neither the fingerprint nor admissibility, so T stays current, which the claim allows. Case (c): the target leaves the graph because a premise far upstream fails admission. The target already depended on that premise in the build before the change, so the claim covers it. For a staged-only node, re-proposing it with new text is a restatement, since DEF-restatement explicitly counts 'staged in the ledger'. I could not build a scenario that satisfies every premise under a fixed reading and breaks the 'only when'.

counterexample: Missing premise: a node's statement and cited premises are those of its candidate under DEF-premise-graph (the declaration if the id is declared at head, otherwise the staged proposal). So a declaration appearing or disappearing beside a staged proposal with the same id and different text restates that node in DEF-restatement's sense.
reasoning: The step relies on a correspondence no cited premise states. DEF-restatement and DEF-current-trial both speak of 'its statement' and 'the premises it cites', but neither says which record supplies them when a declaration and a staged proposal share an id. The derivation also argues that 'the graph changes only when a node is declared, restated or removed' and that 'declaring a new node' affects no trial. Declaring an id that is already staged is not declaring a new node. Deleting a declaration while a proposal with the same id stays staged is neither a declaration nor a removal. These changes fold into 'restated' only if the node's statement and citations are those of its candidate under DEF-premise-graph's precedence. LMA-blast-radius-propagation rests on the same undefined notion of 'restated', so it cannot close the hole.

To derive NOT(claim) I would need a trial that stops being current with no amendment, restatement or removal of its target or upstream nodes. The only candidates are the precedence switches above, and those break the claim only under a per-record reading of 'its statement': the declaration's text never changed, it just vanished, and the staged text never changed either. No cited premise supplies that reading, and DEF-premise-graph's 'a node is identified by its id' weighs against it. So NOT(claim) is not derivable from the premises as worded. The unresolved reading is recorded as the entailment gap, not as symmetric derivability.

Attacks tried against the new identity rules. (1) Id collision: declared id X can't be admitted (it cites a missing premise), and a staged proposal for X cites something present. If the proposal could stand in as a second X, an edge could close back onto an existing X. It can't: a declared id's only candidate is its declaration, whether or not it can be admitted, so the proposal is never a candidate. Even if it were, a node is its id and is admitted at most once. (2) Self-citation: A cites A. A can only be admitted once A is already in the graph, but A isn't in the graph until it's admitted, so A is never admitted and no self-loop appears. (3) Candidate swap mid-build: a proposal for Y is replaced after Y is admitted, and the new version cites Z, which was admitted later. Edges are added only when a node is admitted, from the premises that node cites then, and 'never removes one' plus 'no other step adds a node or an edge' means Y never gets a Z->Y edge later. So admission order is a topological order whatever the candidates are. (4) Mutual citation A<->B: whichever is admitted first needs the other already present, so neither is admitted. No scenario that meets every premise gives a cycle.

The induction rests on four clauses of DEF-premise-graph: the build starts empty; each admission adds a node that is new, because each node is admitted at most once; every edge added in that step runs from a premise already in the graph to the new node; and no other step adds edges or removes anything. So each edge runs from an earlier-admitted node to a later one, and an edge leaving n needs a citing node admitted after n. This covers the self-loop case, because n can't be both new and already present. Nothing in the argument depends on which candidate an id has, so the restated identity rules add no hidden assumption. The claim is only about cited edges, and the definition says those are the only edges. No gap.

Deriving NOT(claim) would need some edge running from a later-admitted node to an earlier one, or a node admitted twice. The definition rules out both: edges are added only at admission, from premises already present, and each node is admitted at most once. The identity clauses (one candidate per id, content taken from the candidate) can only shrink the set of admissible nodes; they add no path to a back-edge. The premises settle the claim positively, so the negation can't be derived.

Replayed the two-proposals-one-id attack. P1 then P2 are proposed for undeclared id X, and P2 cites a missing premise. Under the restated DEF-premise-graph, X has at most one staged proposal, P2, and it is X's only candidate. P1 is no longer a staged node, so it cannot be admitted in X's place and hide P2. The node X (identified by its id) is not admitted, and AXM-no-silent-failure reports it. Variants tried: (a) P2 withdrawn. Whichever way 'most recently proposed and not withdrawn since' is read, at most one proposal is staged and the report covers that one. (b) X is declared at head and also has a staged proposal. The declaration is the only candidate 'whether or not it can be admitted', so a declaration that cannot be admitted makes node X unadmitted and reported as a declared node. The staged proposal's content cannot quietly stand in for it. (c) Build-order dependence. Admission is monotone and a build ends only when every candidate left out cites an absent premise, so every build reaches the same node set, and 'no build admits' coincides with 'cannot take its place in the premise graph'. (d) A branch loses its subject. A subject is not a citation, so it is not an edge (DEF-premise-graph), not part of a fingerprint (DEF-current-trial), and excluded from the proof-state inputs (DEF-proof-state). Place, current trials and proof state are unchanged, and the loss is reported under AXM-no-silent-failure. No scenario satisfied every premise and broke the claim.

Each clause maps to a premise. Entry into the graph comes from DEF-premise-graph (built from head declarations and ledger proposals only). 'No effect as a declaration' comes from AXM-commit-is-approval. The reporting of unadmitted declared or staged nodes, and of subject-less branches, comes from AXM-no-silent-failure. 'Keeps its proof state' comes from DEF-proof-state excluding the subject, DEF-current-trial fingerprints covering only statement and cited premises, and DEF-premise-graph making only citations edges. The one identification needed, 'no build admits' = 'cannot take its place in the premise graph', follows from the build definition: the admitted set is independent of order. The prior gap is closed because one candidate per id means the node that is reported is exactly the node that is missing.

To derive NOT(claim), the premises would have to allow (i) something outside head declarations or staged proposals entering the graph, (ii) a staged proposal taking effect as a declaration, (iii) an unadmitted declared or staged node, or a subject-less branch, going unreported, or (iv) the subject influencing the proof state. (i) contradicts DEF-premise-graph, (ii) AXM-commit-is-approval, (iii) AXM-no-silent-failure, and (iv) DEF-proof-state together with DEF-current-trial. With one candidate per id, a second proposal can no longer be the thing admitted under X, so the old route to (iii) is gone. The premises decide the claim.

subject: DEF-premise-graph
text: Wording ambiguity, not a flaw in BRN-consistency-declarations-gate: 'the one most recently proposed for it and not withdrawn since' can mean either (a) the latest proposal, and only if it has not been withdrawn, or (b) the latest proposal among those not withdrawn, so an older one comes back when the newest is withdrawn. Both readings give at most one staged proposal, so the gate claim holds under either. They differ on whether withdrawing the newest proposal brings an older one back into staging, and the author may want to fix one reading. Separately: when a declared id also has a staged proposal, that proposal's content is never a candidate. AXM-no-silent-failure only reports at node (id) granularity, so being shadowed this way is not reported as such.

reasoning: Attacks tried, all under the restated identity rules. (a) Two versions of one id: X is declared at head as a lemma citing an absent id, and a staged proposal for X cites only a declared axiom. The declaration is X's only candidate even though it cannot be admitted, so the proposal is never considered. X is not admitted, has no proof state and is not proven. (b) Self-citation or mutual citation via proposals: A's candidate cites B and B's cites A. Admission needs every cited premise already in the graph, so neither is admitted and no cycle forms. Since each node is admitted at most once and never removed, and edges come only from already-admitted premises, admission order is a topological order and a cycle is impossible. (c) A staged proposal that looks like an axiom and cites nothing, used as a root: it is admitted, but it is not a *declared* axiom or definition, so any lemma or branch depending on it fails the root condition. (d) A declared axiom that cites a staged, citation-free lemma: the axiom is not a cite-none node, so the check walks on to the staged lemma, which is not declared, and dependents are not proven. (e) A lemma or branch citing nothing: excluded by 'cites at least one premise'. (f) An ancestry ending outside the graph: a node with an unadmitted premise is itself never admitted. Also checked: the order of a build cannot change the outcome. Admission is monotone and a build ends only at closure, so the admitted set is the least fixpoint and does not depend on order. No scenario satisfies every premise and breaks the claim.

Acyclicity comes directly from LMA-kernel-enforces-acyclicity, and it also follows independently from DEF-premise-graph's admission rule, which meets AXM-acyclicity. 'Never proven' when ungrounded comes from DEF-proof-state's two clauses. A node no build admits has no proof state. An admitted lemma or branch needs a citation, and every citation-free node it depends on must be a declared axiom or definition. That is the ungrounded case AXM-axiomatic-grounding forbids. The two definitions agree on which version is read. DEF-premise-graph makes a declared id's declaration its only candidate, and any other id's staged proposal (the most recent, not withdrawn) its only candidate. DEF-proof-state reads exactly that version: the declaration at head, else the staged proposal. The conditions on trials only add requirements, so they cannot turn an ungrounded node into a proven one. The opening clause says the kernel builds the graph as defined. That holds by definition, because DEF-premise-graph defines the premise graph as the kernel's build. Whether the implementation matches is fidelity, carried by the cited evidence CTR-proof-dag-invariants, not by this step. Two assumptions are implicit but harmless to this claim. First, 'the declaration' assumes one declaration per id at head. Second, 'current trials' is undefined in these premises. Neither can let an ungrounded node read as proven.

NOT(claim) would need either a cycle in some build or a proven lemma or branch with a citation-free ancestor that is not a declared axiom or definition. The first contradicts both LMA-kernel-enforces-acyclicity and the only-admit-after-premises rule in DEF-premise-graph. The second contradicts DEF-proof-state's 'exactly when' condition.
