Because the admitted set is a unique least fixpoint, builds cannot diverge, and the proof state is a function of that single graph. So the premises cannot derive the negation.

subject: BRN-dag-integrity
text: Not load-bearing for this claim, but worth tightening. (1) DEF-premise-graph's 'the declaration' assumes one declaration per id at head; the definition never says so. (2) DEF-proof-state uses 'current trials' without defining it in the premises served: it does not say whether trials recorded against a staged proposal's statement count once the id is declared with a different statement. Neither can make an ungrounded node read as proven, because the grounding condition applies independently of the trial conditions.

reasoning: Attacks tried. (1) The several-proposals replay: undeclared id X has proposals P1 then P2, and two builds admit different versions. This now violates DEF-premise-graph. An id has at most one staged proposal, the one most recently proposed and not withdrawn since, and that proposal is its only candidate. Each id therefore has exactly one candidate, fixed by the head-revision declarations and the ledger. With one candidate per id, the admitted set is order-independent. Every admitted node's cited premises were in the graph before it, and a build may not end while a left-out candidate has all its premises in, so every build ends at the same least closed set. (2) A report changes which candidate an id has. It would have to make the id declared or undeclared at head, which needs a declaration change and is barred by DEF-report. Or it would have to change which proposal is most recent or not withdrawn, which needs a proposal or withdrawal appended to the ledger. By DEF-ledger the ledger is its records, so that is appending a record, also barred by DEF-report. (3) A report writes something outside the ledger and declarations. Proof state reads nothing but the graph, the admitted version and the trials on it (DEF-proof-state). The graph's inputs are declarations and staged proposals (DEF-premise-graph). Current-trial status reads validity after amendments, graph membership and fingerprints, and fingerprints are fixed by the candidate's statement and premises (DEF-current-trial, DEF-premise-graph). None of these changes. (4) A report makes existing evidence ineligible, for example a contract no longer measurable by a declared test. That needs a declaration change. Altering a captured artifact is excluded because the ledger, artifacts included, is append-only (DEF-ledger). (5) A report moves HEAD to a revision whose declarations match. The declarations at head are unchanged, so nothing moves. Moving HEAD to a revision whose declarations differ is a declaration change, barred. Every scenario either leaves the claim standing or breaks a premise.

Checked the paraphrases against the current wording. DEF-proof-state: the rationale's 'its declaration at the head revision, or, for an id not declared there, its staged proposal' and 'from nothing else belief.yaml or the ledger says about it' are verbatim. It leaves out 'with that version's statement, cited premises and declared sufficiency', but those belong to the admitted version, which it argues is unchanged, so nothing depends on the omission. DEF-premise-graph: 'built from the axioms, definitions, lemmas and branches declared at the head revision and the proposals staged in the ledger' is verbatim. DEF-current-trial: the rationale shortens the fingerprint clause to 'the fingerprints it recorded'. The dropped half, whether they equal the ones the target and its dependencies have now, still follows. DEF-current-trial fixes a fingerprint by statement and cited premises, and DEF-premise-graph makes those the candidate's, which is unchanged. That step is implicit, not unstated. DEF-belief-eligible: 'a trial record, measured or imported' is faithful. The step 'appending no record, stages or restates no proposal' needs a staged proposal to be a ledger record. DEF-premise-graph says 'staged in the ledger', and DEF-ledger defines the ledger as its records, so that holds. The earlier gap, several proposals per id, is closed by DEF-premise-graph's one-candidate-per-id clause, and with it build-to-build determinism. The finding-is-not-a-record step follows from DEF-report: output appends nothing. No clause needs the implementation.

To derive NOT(claim), some input to a measured belief or a proof state would have to change while a report is produced. Every such input is the head-revision declarations, ledger records (trials, amendments, staged proposals, withdrawals) or quantities fixed by them: which candidate each id has, the admitted set, fingerprints, current-trial status. DEF-report forbids changing any of them. AXM-no-belief-write-path forbids a belief moving without belief-eligible evidence. With one candidate per id, the build's outcome is fixed, so no nondeterminism is left to argue a change from. NOT(claim) is not derivable.

Replayed the prior attack: X declared with statement A and staged with statement B, a trial of T (T depends on X) recorded X's fingerprint of A; delete the declaration. By DEF-premise-graph X's only candidate becomes the staged proposal, so X's statement is now B; X's id stays staged, so by DEF-restatement X is restated (the 'declaration disappears beside a staged proposal' case), and T depends on X in the before-build, so the claim lists this event. The reverse (declaring an already-staged id with different content) is the same case. Other attacks tried: (1) T drops out of the graph with no listed event: T leaves only if a cited premise leaves; by induction on the citation chain some ancestor is removed or restated (including restating to cite T, which forms a cycle, still a restatement of an ancestor in the before-build). The build is a least fixpoint, so it cannot differ between reads with the same records. (2) T's dependency set changes with no restatement: edges come only from cited premises of admitted nodes, so the set changes only if some ancestor's cited premises change, which is a restatement. (3) Withdrawing the latest proposal so that an earlier one, or nothing, becomes the candidate: that is either a restatement (the candidate becomes another record) or a removal. (4) Declaring a new, unstaged id: it cannot be an ancestor of an already-admitted T, since T's citations are unchanged. (5) An amendment to another trial: DEF-current-trial counts only amendments appended to this trial. (6) Fingerprints are not keyed by id, so two nodes can share one, but that can only keep a trial current, never stop it. No scenario satisfies every premise and falsifies the claim.

Sentence 1 follows from DEF-ledger being append-only. Sentence 2: DEF-current-trial makes currency a function of three things. Validity after amendments changes only by an appended amendment. The target's presence in the graph and its dependency set are fixed by candidates' citations (DEF-premise-graph). Fingerprints change only when a statement or cited premises change (DEF-current-trial, DEF-restatement). DEF-premise-graph now fixes whose statement counts (one candidate per id, declaration first), and DEF-restatement explicitly counts a switch of candidate as restating, which closes the earlier gap. LMA-blast-radius-propagation confines the effect to the node and the nodes that depend on it before or after the change. Sentence 3 is DEF-counterexample read against the present premises. One small wording ambiguity: whether an id that moves from declared-only to staged-only in one change 'stays declared or staged' as DEF-restatement requires. Read as membership in the union, it does, so I judge the step sound, not a gap.

To derive NOT(claim), the premises would have to allow either a trial being edited or removed (DEF-ledger forbids it), or a currency loss without an amendment and without the target or an ancestor being restated or removed. Every input to DEF-current-trial reduces to those events, so no such loss can be derived. They would also have to allow a DEF-counterexample that coexists with entailment, which the definition excludes. NOT(claim) is not derivable.

subject: BRN-falsification-trial-ledger
text: Wording nit, no proof weight: DEF-restatement's phrase 'while its id stays declared at the head revision or staged in the ledger' would be clearer if it said explicitly that it means membership in the union throughout the change. Then an id whose declaration is deleted while a proposal is staged in the same change is plainly restated, not ambiguously removed-then-added. Also, DEF-premise-graph's 'most recently proposed for it and not withdrawn since' leaves open whether withdrawing the latest proposal makes an earlier one the candidate again. Either reading is covered by restatement or removal, so the claim is unaffected.

reasoning: Attacks tried. (1) Sentence 1, where r's restatement makes r cite a missing premise or form a cycle, so r and everything citing it drop out of the graph: the trials of its dependents fail DEF-current-trial because their target is not in the graph. Where the target is still admitted but no longer depends on r, the recorded set holds r and the current set does not, so it is not 'exactly those'. (2) Fingerprint collision: a recorded fingerprint of r happens to equal another node's current one. This fails under the natural per-node reading of 'the fingerprints ... of its target and of each node its target then depended on'. (3) Sentence 3 with e in neither build, or with e depending on r only in some historical trial's recorded set: the trial is not current in either build, so its status is unchanged. (4) Sentence 3 re-admission: the DEF-premise-graph end condition gives induction on the first build's admission order. The earliest ancestor of e left out of the other build would have all its premises in, which contradicts the end condition. So e and its ancestors are re-admitted with identical candidates and fingerprints. (5) Removal of a declared r that still has a staged proposal: the proposal becomes r's candidate, but the claim's own clause 'neither declared nor staged' excludes this. (6) Strongest: a bundled change. One revision removes r and also restates n1 (which cited r) back to an earlier statement that does not cite r. A trial T of n2 (which cites n1) recorded {n2, n1-old} before n1 ever cited r. T was not current before the change and is current after it, although n2 depended on r before. Bundling also breaks sentence 3 trivially: restate an unrelated e alongside r. This refutes the claim only if 'when r is restated/removed' allows other ids' candidates to change in the same step. The claim's 'the change' reads as r's change alone, so I record this attack as the entailment gap, not as a falsification.

counterexample: Unstated premise: a restatement of r replaces r's candidate (its declaration at head or, if undeclared, its staged proposal) and changes no other id's candidate; a removal likewise changes only r. This could come from citing DEF-restatement, or from stating the confinement in the claim ('when r's candidate alone is restated/removed').
reasoning: Sentence 1 does not depend on what 'restated' means. For any change, a trial that recorded a fingerprint of r other than r's current one is not current by DEF-current-trial, and DEF-premise-graph now fixes r's fingerprint as its candidate's. Sentences 2 and 3 do depend on it. The path induction for removal and the re-admission argument for e both rest on the derivation's 'since only r changed': every other id keeps the same candidate, with the same statement and cited premises. The restated DEF-premise-graph makes each id's candidate a function of that id's own declaration or staged proposal. It does not define a restatement or removal of r as a change to r's declaration or proposal alone. DEF-restatement, which might, is not cited. The event also remains ambiguous. Staging a new proposal for a declared r leaves r's candidate, and so its fingerprint, unchanged. If 'restated' covered that event and 'r's new one' meant the proposal's fingerprint, sentence 1 would call current trials not current. The cited premises cannot rule that reading out.

Can NOT(claim) be derived from the cited premises? That would need a scenario forced by DEF-current-trial, DEF-premise-graph and the axiom in which a confined change to r leaves a stale-fingerprint trial current, makes a dependent of a removed r current, or changes the status of a non-dependent's trial. None exists: under the confined reading all three sentences follow, per the counterexample trial. The bundled-change scenario shows only that the claim is not derivable without the confinement premise. It does not show that the negation is derivable, so the premises do not support both the claim and its negation.

Attack: a change that alters several candidates at once. Trial T targets X, current before the change, and no node in D_before(X) or D_after(X) (or X itself) is restated or removed. (1) Newly admitted node N joins D_after(X): a path N -> ... -> X in the after build ends at X, whose citations did not change. Walk it backwards: each node on it is in D_after, so it was not restated and cites what it cited before. X was in the before graph, so by DEF-premise-graph every premise X cites was too, and so on back along the path. So N was in the before graph and in D_before. That contradicts N being new. The same walk rules out gaining a dependency through another node's restatement: that node would lie on the path and be in D_after, so it is excluded by hypothesis. (2) X leaves the graph: every node in D_before keeps its candidate content. By induction from the sources, all of D_before and X are admitted again, because the end state of a monotone build is the unique least closure, whatever the order of admission. (3) Fingerprint mismatch: a fingerprint is a function of statement and cited premises, and those are unchanged on D_before = D_after and on X. (4) Legacy trials with no fingerprints can only fail through (2). (5) A candidate swapped for a record with the same content changes no fingerprint and no edge. No scenario satisfies every premise and breaks the 'only when'. Sentences 1 and 3 follow directly from DEF-ledger (append-only) and DEF-counterexample.

The trial-by-trial clause in the rule rests only on DEF-current-trial's three conditions. The fingerprint is determined by statement and cited premises. Admission is monotone, from DEF-premise-graph. Restatement and removal are defined as a change of candidate content, or the id leaving both sources. LMA-blast-radius-propagation is no longer needed for the multi-candidate case, so its narrowing to one node r leaves no hole. The rule's step 'its target now depends on a node it did not ... needs some node its target depends on after the change to be restated' is not argued in the text. It does follow from the backward-path argument: an unrestated node on a new path cites what it cited before, and admission before the change forces its premises into the before graph. The uniqueness of the build result is implicit, but it follows from the stated admission and termination rules. 'Validity changes only by an appended amendment' follows from DEF-ledger: the recorded trial is never edited, and DEF-current-trial reads validity only after amendments. No clause needs the implementation.

NOT(claim) would need a trial that stops being current with no amendment and no restatement or removal in X or D_before(X) or D_after(X), or a recorded trial that is edited, or a DEF-counterexample that fails to show non-entailment. The first is ruled out by the argument above, the second by DEF-ledger's append-only rule, and the third by DEF-counterexample's own wording: every premise holds and the claim fails. None of these can be derived from the premises.

Attacks tried. (1) The old combined attack (remove r and restate a dependent d so it no longer cites r, bringing back an old trial of d): the new scope excludes it if restating d counts as changing d's candidate. (2) A staged proposal for a declared r: the declaration is r's only candidate, so editing or withdrawing the proposal does not restate r. Deleting the declaration so the proposal with the same content takes over changes r's candidate but not r's statement or citations. That is neither a restatement nor a removal, so the change is out of scope and the lemma claims nothing. (3) Dependents that gain or lose r: a path from r runs through nodes that cite r, and their citations are fixed. So only r's own admission can change who depends on r (r restated to cite a missing premise, or to cite its own dependent and form a cycle). Every node this touches depends on r in one of the two builds, so clause 3 excludes it. (4) Clause 3 induction: if e is admitted, its whole ancestor closure is admitted and acyclic and does not contain r. The same candidates give the same closure and the same fingerprints in the other build, and a build admits every node whose ancestors are all admitted. That holds. Two scenarios do break the claim, but each needs a contested reading, so I recorded them as the entailment gap and not as a falsification. (a) One commit restates r and also edits the declaration of an unrelated e. e's candidate is still its declaration, but its content changed, so e's trials go stale and clause 3 fails. The same move rebuilds the combined attack: remove r and edit d's declaration back to an older statement that does not cite r, and an old trial of d is current again, so clause 2 fails. (b) Fingerprints collide across ids: X depends on r, s and t, with fp(r)=fp(s)=A and fp(t)=B before the change. r is restated so fp(r)=B. The recorded collection {fx,A,B} equals the current {fx,B,A}, so under a collection reading the trial stays current and clause 1 fails.

counterexample: Needed premises: (a) 'changes no other id's candidate' means that no other id's statement or cited premises change, and no id gains or loses a candidate; that is, no id other than r is restated or removed as DEF-restatement defines them. (b) DEF-current-trial matches recorded fingerprints node by node, keyed by id, and does not compare them as a collection.
reasoning: There are two unstated assumptions. (1) DEF-restatement separates a candidate whose own content changes from a candidate that becomes another record, so 'changes no other id's candidate' can be read as 'no other id's candidate becomes another record'. That reading still allows an edit to another declaration's text. The derivation's step 'the other build gives e ... the same candidate, ... the same fingerprints' needs the content to be the same, not just the record. (2) The derivation paraphrases DEF-current-trial as comparing 'the one it recorded for r' with 'r's fingerprint now', which is a node-by-node match by id. But DEF-current-trial says only that the recorded fingerprints 'are exactly those' the nodes have now, and it makes a fingerprint depend on statement and citations alone, without the id. So two distinct nodes can share a fingerprint, and a comparison of collections can pass after r is restated. The other paraphrases are faithful: removal leaves no candidate, admission needs every cited premise, a restatement changes the fingerprint, and a node outside the graph means the trial is not current.

Under readings the premises allow, NOT(claim) can be derived. If a candidate may keep its record while its content changes, a commit that restates r and edits an independent e's declaration makes e's trials stop being current, which contradicts clause 3. Under the collection reading of 'exactly those', the r/s/t fingerprint collision keeps a trial current even though it recorded r's old fingerprint, which contradicts clause 1. Under the id-keyed, content-fixed readings the claim holds. So the premises as worded do not decide it.

I tried to build a scenario where every premise holds, the subject of branch B is removed from belief.yaml by a commit, and B's proof state still changes. For that to happen, the subject would have to reach one of the four inputs DEF-proof-state allows. (a) Place in the graph: under DEF-premise-graph, a node is admitted only because of the premises it cites, and only a citation is an edge. The subject is not cited, so B's admission and its dependencies are unchanged. (b) Admitted version and declared sufficiency: removing the subject from belief.yaml is a change to belief.yaml, not to B's declaration or staged proposal. The only candidate for B's id is unchanged, and so are its statement, premises and sufficiency. (c) Which trials are current, attacked through the id-for-id rule: the recorded ids are B and the nodes B depended on. Losing the subject adds or removes no citation, so the set of ids is the same now. Each fingerprint is determined by statement and cited premises, so it is a function of those two alone, and neither changed, so every fingerprint matches id for id. A trial without fingerprints is current whatever the subject is. Validity changes only through appended amendments, and losing a subject is not an amendment. B stays in the graph. (d) Anything else: DEF-proof-state excludes the subject by name. I then replayed the attacks on unadmitted nodes that are never reported. First, a staged proposal hidden behind a declaration of the same id: it is not a node, because a node is its id and the declaration is that id's only candidate. So the claim does not require it to be reported. Second, a node whose declaration cannot be admitted, or a node in a citation cycle: none is ever admitted. AXM-no-silent-failure requires such a node to be reported, and because builds only add nodes and stop at closure, 'no build admits it' coincides with 'cannot take its place'. Third, a branch that loses its subject and is also unadmitted: it had no proof state, it keeps none, and AXM-no-silent-failure still requires it to be reported. None of these scenarios breaks the claim.

I checked each clause against a premise. The graph contents come from DEF-premise-graph. That a staged proposal is not a declaration comes from AXM-commit-is-approval. Reporting comes from AXM-no-silent-failure, where 'no build admits' is read as 'cannot take its place'; the two coincide because the build is monotone and closes, so every build admits the same set. That the proof state is kept comes from DEF-proof-state, which names the subject as excluded, together with DEF-current-trial, where each fingerprint is determined by statement and premises alone, so the id-for-id comparison sees no change. I looked for an assumed link from the subject to the statement, the ids, the validity of trials or the declared sufficiency, and found none. The premises treat the subject as separate data outside all of these.

To derive 'losing the subject changes the proof state', the subject would have to reach one of these: admission, the edges, the admitted version, a fingerprint's inputs, the set of dependency ids, or the validity of a trial. It reaches none of them. A fingerprint is a function of statement and premises, and DEF-proof-state excludes the subject by name. Deriving 'an unadmitted declared or staged node goes unreported' would contradict AXM-no-silent-failure. The negation cannot be derived.

Attack 1 (id-for-id fingerprints): I looked for a report that makes a trial's recorded fingerprints stop matching, or start matching, the ones its target and dependencies have now. Under DEF-current-trial that needs one of three things: the set of ids the target now depends on changes, some node's statement or cited premises change, or the recorded fingerprints change. The recorded fingerprints sit in an append-only ledger (DEF-ledger), and a report appends nothing (DEF-report). A node's fingerprint is determined only by its statement and cited premises, and by DEF-premise-graph those belong to the node's candidate: its declaration at head, or its staged proposal. A report changes no declaration and appends no record, so it neither stages nor withdraws a proposal. So every candidate, statement, citation, edge and dependency set stays the same, and the id-for-id comparison gives the same answer. Attack 2: a report that moves the repository head but leaves every declaration unchanged. The premise graph reads only the declarations at head, so nothing changes. Attack 3: build order. With one candidate per id and admission requiring every cited premise already in the graph, the finished build is the unique set of nodes whose citations are all grounded, so the same inputs give the same graph. Attack 4 (validity): validity after amendments depends on amendments, and a report appends none. None of these produces a scenario where every premise holds and some belief or proof state moves.

Checked the rationale's paraphrase against the exact new wording. The paraphrase says currency 'depends on its validity after amendments, its target being in the premise graph, and the fingerprints it recorded'. That is incomplete. It leaves out the other side of the comparison, the fingerprints the target and the nodes it now depends on have now, compared id for id with the same ids and the same fingerprint per id. It also leaves out the case of a trial that recorded no fingerprints. The step still goes through from cited premises alone. 'Leaves the graph unchanged' together with DEF-premise-graph fixes the dependency set and each node's candidate, so it fixes each node's statement and citations. DEF-current-trial ('determined by its statement and the premises it cites') then fixes each current fingerprint. So the omission is loose wording, not an unstated assumption. The belief half needs belief-eligible evidence to be a ledger record, and DEF-belief-eligible (a trial record) with DEF-ledger (trials, for both servers) supplies that. The staging half needs a staged proposal to be ledger content, and DEF-premise-graph's 'proposals staged in the ledger' supplies that, with append-only and 'appends no record' covering any record type. The derivation should name the current-fingerprint side explicitly, but no premise is missing.

I tried to derive NOT(claim), that some report changes a measured belief or a proof state. By AXM-no-belief-write-path a belief moves only through belief-eligible evidence, which is a ledger trial record. By DEF-proof-state a proof state is computed only from the graph, the admitted version, declared sufficiency and the trials recorded on the node, with currency governed by DEF-current-trial. All of these inputs are functions of the declarations and the ledger, and by DEF-report a report changes neither. No premise lets a reader's output feed any of these inputs, so the negation cannot be derived.

subject: BRN-monitor-moves-nothing
text: The derivation paraphrases DEF-current-trial as depending on 'validity after amendments, its target being in the premise graph, and the fingerprints it recorded'. That misses the other side of the new id-for-id comparison: the fingerprints the target and the nodes it NOW depends on have now, compared id for id. It also misses the case of a trial that recorded no fingerprints. The conclusion still follows because 'graph unchanged' fixes those. The author might restate the rationale so it says: a report leaves each node's candidate, and so its statement, citations and dependency set, unchanged, so every current fingerprint and every id set compared is unchanged.

reasoning: Attacks tried, each from the premises only, assuming a trial of T that was current just before a change. (1) Multi-id change: declare P (new id) and restate unrelated U together. By DEF-premise-graph the build is order-independent (the first node of one maximal build missing from another would have all premises present, violating the end condition), so every old ancestor of T keeps an unchanged candidate unless restated/removed, and by induction is re-admitted with the same citations; T stays in the graph with the same ancestor set and, since a fingerprint is determined by statement and cited premises, the same fingerprints id for id. The trial stays current. (2) Newly declared id admitting a node: for T to gain it as an ancestor, some node on the new path to T must cite it; walking back from T through unchanged nodes stays inside the old ancestor set, so the first node that cites outside it had its cited premises change and is restated under DEF-restatement -- an ancestor in the before-build. (3) Recorded id set differs from current one: lost ids require an old ancestor restated (citations changed) or removed; gained ids reduce to (2). (4) Target leaving the graph with no ancestor touched: impossible by the re-admission induction in (1). (5) Candidate swap with identical content (declaration appearing beside a staged proposal): not a restatement, fingerprints unchanged, trial stays current -- consistent with the claim. (6) Legacy trial with no fingerprints: can only stop being current by amendment or target leaving the graph, both covered. No scenario satisfies every premise while a trial stops being current outside the listed causes.

DEF-current-trial makes currency a function of (validity after appended amendments, target membership in the graph, recorded fingerprints vs. present fingerprints id for id). DEF-ledger makes the trial record append-only, so validity moves only by an appended amendment. DEF-premise-graph fixes the build as the unique least closure of candidates under citation (order-independence follows from the admission and end rules), so membership and ancestor sets change only through a change in some candidate's content or existence, which DEF-restatement names restating or removing. Fingerprints change only with statement or cited premises (DEF-current-trial). The multi-id case is argued directly in the derivation, not by stacking LMA-blast-radius-propagation, and each branch of it (amendment, target leaves graph, fingerprint differs, id set differs) reduces to a restatement or removal of T or an ancestor in the before or after build. The last sentence follows directly from DEF-counterexample. The first sentence follows from DEF-ledger and AXM-falsifiable-measurement. I found no clause that needs knowledge of the implementation.

NOT(claim) would require a trial that stops being current with no amendment and no restatement/removal of T or any before/after ancestor. Under the premises, an unchanged ancestor closure is re-admitted identically with identical fingerprints, so DEF-current-trial's three conditions keep holding; the negation cannot be derived. The negation of the non-edit clause contradicts DEF-ledger's append-only record, and the negation of the last sentence contradicts DEF-counterexample. The premises decide the claim.

Replayed both prior attacks. (1) Editing another id x's declaration in place alongside r: if x's statement or cited premises change while x stays declared, that is a restatement of x by DEF-restatement, which the scope now excludes; if only content outside statement and cited premises changes, x's fingerprint is unchanged because a fingerprint is determined by statement and cited premises, so no clause moves. (2) A fingerprint collision between r and another node y: DEF-current-trial now compares id for id, so a recorded fingerprint under id y is never matched against r's, and a collision across ids cannot make a stale trial current. A collision of r with its own old fingerprint is ruled out because the fingerprint 'differs whenever either differs'. New attacks. (3) A candidate switches to a record with identical content (declaration of x deleted with an identical staged proposal beside it): x keeps a candidate, is not restated, and statement, citations, admission and fingerprint are all unchanged; DEF-current-trial does not read declared-vs-staged. (4) Withdrawing a staged proposal shadowed by a declaration: the candidate is unchanged. (5) An id losing its candidate: by DEF-premise-graph that happens exactly when the id is neither declared nor staged, which is removal and excluded unless it is r. (6) Restated r that no longer admits, or that the target stops depending on: the recorded id r is missing from the current id set, so the trial is not current anyway. (7) Clause 3 for an e admitted in only one build: the admitted set is the well-founded closure, which is unique given the candidates, so it cannot differ on r-free ancestry. (8) A cyclic r: a cycle is never admitted, and the argument does not need acyclicity. None of these satisfies the premises and scope while breaking a clause. The only break I found (an amendment appended to a trial of e in the same change) depends on reading the scope narrowly, so I record it as the entailment gap and not as a falsification.

counterexample: Unstated assumption: the change appends no amendment to any trial (and clause 3 ranges only over trials that existed before the change). The scope should add something like 'no trial is recorded or amended'.
reasoning: Clauses 1 and 2 follow: id-for-id comparison plus 'differs whenever either differs' gives clause 1; no candidate for r, plus admission only after every cited premise is in the graph, applied along each path of unchanged citations, gives clause 2. Clause 3 follows on the node side, since the r-free ancestry has identical candidates in both builds, so the same admission, edges and fingerprints. But by DEF-current-trial a trial's currency also depends on 'its validity, after any amendments appended to it', and the claim's scope is spelled out after the colon only in terms of ids: no other id restated or removed, no new candidate. Nothing in the scope fixes the trial ledger. A change that restates r and also appends an amendment reclassifying a valid trial of an unrelated e as invalid (or the reverse) meets every listed condition and flips that trial's currency, which breaks clause 3. The derivation's 'each of e's trials is current exactly as it was' silently assumes validity is held fixed. The words 'and nothing else' could be read to cover this, but the colon gloss that defines them does not. A smaller point of the same kind: 'each of its trials' should be limited to trials that existed before the change, because a trial recorded during the change has no earlier currency to preserve.

I tried to derive NOT(claim) from the premises. For clauses 1 and 2 the negation would need a stale fingerprint of r to match, or a removed r (or something downstream of it) to be admitted, and DEF-current-trial and DEF-premise-graph each rule that out. For clause 3 the negation would need an r-free ancestor of e to change its candidate, admission or fingerprint, and the scope forbids every such node-level change. The one route to the negation is an amendment to a trial of e, which depends on how the claim's own scope is read, not on anything the premises leave undecided. It is recorded as the entailment gap, not here.
